title: 43. Pulmonary arterial pressure as a predictor of performance in beef calves across weaning and preconditioning strategies.
content:
Abstract
Bovine respiratory disease (BRD) presents a significant challenge to the sustainability of beef production, with incidence often heighted during the weaning period. Potential damage to the pulmonary system resulting from BRD may increase the risk of pulmonary hypertension and subsequently bovine congestive heart failure in affected animals. Because stress and BRD risk are elevated at weaning, management practices during this time is critical to mitigate the impact on the long-term health of the animal. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate pulmonary arterial pressure (PAP) as a predictor of performance on weaning strategy and pre-weaning vaccination. A total of 55 crossbred steers from the University of Wyoming Beef Unit herd were stratified into a 2 x 2 factorial design where animals were assigned to one of four treatment groups: no preconditioning with immediate weaning, preconditioning with immediate weaning, no preconditioning with fenceline weaning, and preconditioning with fenceline weaning. Steers received respiratory and clostridial vaccines 45 d prior to weaning (preconditioning only) and at weaning (d 0; preconditioning and no preconditioning). After weaning, steers were fed for 100 days through the Vytelle SENSE bunks, and PAP was measured at the beginning (d 16) and end (d 100) of the study. The PROC GLM and PROC REG procedures in SAS were utilized to evaluate the data with PAP values being a predictor for performance. The linear model showed a tendency for weaning weight to be significant (P = 0.06) where preconditioned calves were heavier than calves that were not preconditioned (P = 0.02). The regression model was significant where the change in PAP over time, initial PAP, and final PAP influenced RFI (-0.03, -0.86, 0.97 respectively; P ≤ 0.003) in the preconditioned and fenceline weaned group. The regression model tended to be significant for weaning weight where initial PAP was the only significant indicator within the preconditioned and immediate wean group (38.93; P = 0.02). These data indicate that preconditioning can potentially improve weaning weights. Additionally, PAP can be used as a predictor for performance variables in preconditioned fenceline weaned steers, but this did not hold true for those that were immediately weaned. More research is needed to determine if these results remain true in other cohorts of animals.
